etymology: Hebrew ‘ein-rimmon, “fountain of the pomegranate,” from ‘ayin, a fountain or spring, joined to rimmon, the pomegranate, a place of the south country of Judah.
biblical_def: En-rimmon lies in the south country of Judah, a fountain named for the pomegranate that grew beside its waters. In the days of Joshua the inheritance of Judah numbered Ain and Rimmon as cities of the uttermost south (Josh 15:32), and these two, set together by the one spring, came in after time to be known as the single town En-rimmon, “the fountain of the pomegranate.” It is named among the places which the children of Judah dwelt in after the captivity, when the LORD brought again His people out of Babylon and set them in their cities: “And at En-rimmon, and at Zareah, and at Jarmuth” (Neh 11:29). Thus a fountain of the dry south, lost for the seventy years of exile, was reinhabited by the returning remnant, and the smoke of dwelling went up again where water springs in a thirsty land. The pomegranate was a fruit of the goodly land and a figure wrought in gold upon the hem of the high priest and upon the pillars of the temple. En-rimmon, a fountain hung about with that fruit, witnesses that the LORD plants His people beside waters, and that He who scattered His remnant for their sin gathers them again to the wells He digged for their fathers, that they might drink and not faint.
webster_summary: A place of the south of Judah, “fountain of the pomegranate,” reinhabited after the captivity.

etymology: Hebrew ‘ein-tappūach, “fountain of Tappuah” or “fountain of the apple,” from ‘ayin, a spring, with tappūach, the apple, a place upon the border of Manasseh.
biblical_def: En-tappuah is the fountain of the land of Tappuah, set upon the border that parted the inheritance of Manasseh from Ephraim. When Joshua divided the land by lot, the coast of Manasseh ran out “unto the inhabitants of En-tappuah” (Josh 17:7), and the Scripture is careful to mark how the land of Tappuah belonged to Manasseh, but the city Tappuah itself, upon the border, fell to the children of Ephraim (Josh 17:8). Thus a single spring became a landmark of the inheritance, a token set in the ground by which the bounds of two tribes were known. The name signifies the fountain of the apple, a watered place where the apple tree might grow and bear among the goodly fruits of the hill country. It is a quiet witness of how the LORD parted the land among the tribes of Israel, and set fast the lines of every man’s heritage by sure marks of water and of stone. The fountains of the land were not lightly named; they were the means of life in the high country, and the LORD wove them into the very surveying of the inheritance. En-tappuah stands that the reader may know how God measured out to each tribe its portion, and made even a spring of the apple a boundary of the promised land, that none might remove his neighbour’s landmark which the fathers had set.

etymology: Hebrew ‘ein-shemesh, “fountain of the sun,” from ‘ayin, a spring, with shemesh, the sun, a spring upon the border between Judah and Benjamin.
biblical_def: En-shemesh, “the fountain of the sun,” is a spring set upon the border that ran between the inheritance of Judah and the inheritance of Benjamin, eastward of Jerusalem upon the way that goeth down toward Jericho. When Joshua marked the bounds of Judah, the border “went up toward Debir from the valley of Achor, and so northward, looking toward Gilgal… and the border passed toward the waters of En-shemesh” (Josh 15:7). The same fountain stands again in the surveying of Benjamin’s coast: “and went forth toward the waters of Enshemesh, and the goings out thereof were at En-rogel” (Josh 18:17). Thus the fountain of the sun, lying low upon the road that climbs from Jericho to the holy city, was a sure mark of the dividing of two tribes, and a spring of water for them that journeyed up to Zion. The men of old named it for the sun, perhaps because its eastward face caught the first light of the morning as it rose over the wilderness of Judah. It is a place without story of its own, yet it served the pilgrim going up to the house of God, who found water at the fountain of the sun on his way to the courts of the LORD. En-shemesh witnesses that God set wells of refreshing upon the road that leads to His sanctuary, that His people might pass through the dry country and not faint until they appear before Him in Zion.

etymology: Hebrew ‘ein-haqqōre’, “the well of him that cried,” or “the fountain of the caller,” from ‘ayin, a spring, with the participle of qārā’, to call or cry, the spring God clave in Lehi for Samson.
biblical_def: En-hakkore is the well that the LORD clave open in Lehi to revive Samson when he was ready to die of thirst. Having smitten a thousand Philistines with the jawbone of an ass, the strong man was sore athirst, and he called on the LORD, and said, “Thou hast given this great deliverance into the hand of thy servant: and now shall I die for thirst, and fall into the hand of the uncircumcised?” (Judg 15:18). And God answered, and “clave an hollow place that was in the jaw, and there came water thereout; and when he had drunk, his spirit came again, and he revived: wherefore he called the name thereof Enhakkore” (Judg 15:19). The name itself preaches: it is the well of him that cried, a memorial that the LORD heard the cry of His servant in his extremity, and brought water out of the dry bone. Samson, a man of many failings, is yet here a man of prayer, who in his thirst looked not to his own strength but cried to the God who had given him the victory; and the God who never breaks the bruised reed answered him with a fountain. En-hakkore witnesses that the LORD is nigh unto all them that call upon Him, that He openeth springs for His fainting people, and that no man who cries to Him in the day of his thirst shall be put to shame.

etymology: Hebrew ‘ein-‘eglāyim, “fountain of the two calves” or “spring of the heifers,” from ‘ayin, a spring, with ‘egel, a calf, a place upon the shore of the Salt Sea.
biblical_def: En-eglaim is named in the vision the LORD gave to Ezekiel of the waters that issue out from under the threshold of the house of God, and run down eastward into the desert, and go into the sea, that the waters of the Dead Sea might be healed (Eze 47:8-9). For where that sea lay accursed and dead, holding no living thing, the river of the sanctuary should bring life, “and it shall come to pass, that the fishers shall stand upon it from En-gedi even unto En-eglaim; they shall be a place to spread forth nets; their fish shall be according to their kinds, as the fish of the great sea, exceeding many” (Eze 47:10). En-eglaim, the fountain of the calves, marks the bound of that healing, a spring upon the salt shore where the prophet beheld nets spread and a multitude of fish where none could live before. It is a place named only here, set in a vision of the age to come, when the waters of grace shall flow from the temple and quicken what was dead. The barren sea is the world dead in trespasses; the river is the Spirit poured out from the riven side of Christ, the true temple; and the fishers spreading their nets are they that take men alive in the gospel net. En-eglaim witnesses that there is no sea so salt but where His river comes, everything shall live whither the river cometh.

En-eglaim stands as a witness that there is no death so deep but the living water of God can quicken it.

etymology: Hebrew ‘ein-chaddāh, “swift fountain” or “sharp spring,” from ‘ayin, a spring, with a root signifying that which is swift or keen, a city upon the border of Issachar.
biblical_def: En-haddah is a city of the inheritance of Issachar, named in the roll of cities that fell to that tribe when Joshua divided the land by lot in Shiloh before the LORD. The fourth lot came out to Issachar, and its coast reached by Jezreel, and Chesulloth, and Shunem, and after the rest of its towns the Scripture sets down “And Remeth, and En-gannim, and En-haddah, and Beth-pazzez” (Josh 19:21). The name is read “swift fountain” or “sharp spring,” a fountain whose waters ran with a keen and ready flow, named perhaps for the strength of its rising. Of any deed done at En-haddah the Scripture says nothing; it is a name in the survey, a spring numbered among the heritage of Issachar, the tribe of whom Jacob said it was a strong ass couching down between two burdens, and of whom it was after said they were men that had understanding of the times, to know what Israel ought to do (1Ch 12:32). Yet the dictionary honours that the Spirit of God set down even this small fountain by name, for it was part of the goodly land which the LORD swore unto the fathers to give their seed. En-haddah witnesses that the God who measured out the inheritance of His people gave them springs of water in their cities, that they might dwell in the land and drink, and bless the LORD their God for the good land which He had given them.

etymology: Hebrew be’ēr ’ēlīm, “well of the mighty” or “well of heroes,” from be’ēr, a well, with ’ēlīm, mighty ones, a place of Moab.
biblical_def: Beer-elim, “the well of the mighty,” is a place upon the border of Moab, named by Isaiah in the burden which the LORD laid upon that proud nation. As the prophet sets forth the wailing that should go up from city to city when judgment came upon Moab, he says, “For the cry is gone round about the borders of Moab; the howling thereof unto Eglaim, and the howling thereof unto Beer-elim” (Isa 15:8). Thus the well of the mighty marks the uttermost bound to which the lamentation of stricken Moab should reach. The name itself joins a well of water to the mighty men or heroes, perhaps a fountain about which the strong of the land once gathered. Some have thought it the same well of which it was said in the wilderness, “Spring up, O well” (Num 21:16-18), for it lay in that border country east of the Salt Sea. Whether the same or another, Beer-elim stands in Isaiah as a witness against the pride of Moab, that strong and self-trusting people who magnified themselves against the LORD. Moab was at ease from his youth, and trusted in the multitude of his mighty men; but the cry of judgment went even unto the well of the heroes, and their strength availed them nothing in the day of the LORD’s visitation. Beer-elim warns that no well of the mighty can quench the thirst of a proud heart, and that the strength of man is broken before God.
webster_summary: A place of Moab, “well of the mighty,” named in Isaiah’s burden of Moab.

corruption_paragraphs: Beer-elim is a place of Moab, named in Isaiah’s burden as a bound of the nation’s howling under the hand of God. Here the Scripture speaks of a real corruption, not invented but plain: the pride of Moab, who was at ease from his youth and trusted in his own strength and the multitude of his mighty men, magnifying himself against the LORD.

The well of the mighty could not save the proud. Moab’s strong men and heroes availed nothing when the cry of judgment came round about his borders, for the strength of man is broken before God. The principle to recover is the LORD’s alone right to give the living water, and the vanity of every proud heart that seeks to quench its thirst at the wells of its own might. He that drinketh of the water that Christ shall give shall never thirst (Joh 4:14); but the proud who trust in their own heroes drink and thirst again, and perish in the day of visitation.

etymology: Hebrew be’ēr lachai rō’ī, “the well of the Living One that seeth me,” from be’ēr, a well, with chai, living, and rō’ī, that seeth me, the well where the angel found Hagar.
biblical_def: Beer-lahai-roi is the well in the wilderness of Shur where the angel of the LORD found Hagar, the handmaid of Sarai, when she fled from her mistress’s face. There the LORD spake unto her and promised that He would multiply her seed exceedingly, and Hagar, in wonder that she had seen and been seen of God, “called the name of the LORD that spake unto her, Thou God seest me: for she said, Have I also here looked after him that seeth me?” (Gen 16:13). And so the well took its name: “Wherefore the well was called Beer-lahai-roi” (Gen 16:14), the well of the Living One that seeth me. It was no place of Israel’s might nor of any battle, but a fountain in a lonely desert where a forsaken bondwoman met the seeing God and lived. This same well became dear to Isaac, the son of promise, for he dwelt by it (Gen 24:62), and after Abraham’s death, “Isaac dwelt by the well Lahai-roi” (Gen 25:11). Thus the well of the seeing God watered the meditations of the heir of the covenant. Beer-lahai-roi witnesses that the God of all the earth seeth the afflicted in their hidden places, that He is the Living One in whose sight no sufferer is forgotten, and that the well at which the cast-out drank is the same fountain by which the children of promise dwell. He who saw Hagar in the wilderness sees His people still.
webster_summary: The well where the angel found Hagar, “the well of him that liveth and seeth me,” by which Isaac dwelt.
webster_full: BEER-LAHAI-ROI, a well in the wilderness, signifying “the well of the Living One that seeth me.”
There the angel of the LORD found Hagar fleeing from Sarai.
Hagar called the name of the LORD, Thou God seest me.
Isaac came from this well and dwelt by it in the south country.
It witnesses that the Living God seeth the afflicted in their hidden places.

corruption_paragraphs: Beer-lahai-roi is the well of the seeing God, named by Hagar in the wilderness of Shur, and no movement of the present age has troubled itself to redefine it. The dictionary records it that the reader who meets the name in the book of Genesis may know it for a real fountain where a forsaken bondwoman met the God who saw her and lived.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the all-seeing care of the Living God for His afflicted, and His provision of living water for the thirsting. He who found Hagar at the well and gave her water and a word of promise is the same who saith, When the poor and needy seek water, and there is none, I the LORD will hear them, I the God of Israel will not forsake them (Isa 41:17). The well of the Living One that seeth me is a faint figure of Him who said unto the woman at another well, Whosoever drinketh of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst (Joh 4:14). He who saw Hagar sees His people still, and brings them to the fountain of living waters.
roots_summary: From the Hebrew for “the well of the Living One that seeth me,” Beer-lahai-roi names the well where the angel found Hagar.

usage: Like Hagar at Beer-lahai-roi, the afflicted soul is found of the God who seeth in secret.
The Living One who saw the cast-out bondwoman forgets none of His thirsting people.
The well at which the forsaken drank is the same fountain by which the children of promise dwell.

etymology: Hebrew be’ēr, “a well,” here a proper name; a station of Israel where the LORD gave them water, and a town whither Jotham fled.
biblical_def: Beer, simply “the well,” is the name of a station of Israel beyond Arnon, where the LORD gave His people water and they sang for joy. “And from thence they went to Beer: that is the well whereof the LORD spake unto Moses, Gather the people together, and I will give them water” (Num 21:16). Then Israel sang this song, “Spring up, O well; sing ye unto it: the princes digged the well, the nobles of the people digged it, by the direction of the lawgiver, with their staves” (Num 21:17-18). It is one of the few songs of the wilderness, a song over water, when the thirsting host saw the LORD bring forth a fountain in the desert. This same name Beer is borne also by a town whither Jotham, the youngest son of Gideon, fled and dwelt for fear of Abimelech his brother, after he had spoken his parable of the trees (Judg 9:21). The place, the well, is a memorial of the kindness of God to His thirsting people. He did not give them water grudgingly, but drew from them a song; and the digging of the well by the staves of the princes shows that the LORD is pleased to use the obedience of His people in bringing forth the streams of His grace. Beer witnesses that where God gathers His people and gives them water, there shall be singing.
webster_summary: The station where the LORD gave Israel water and they sang “Spring up, O well”; also a town whither Jotham fled.

A town of the same name was the refuge of Jotham from Abimelech (Judg 9:21).

corruption_paragraphs: Beer, the well, is a station of Israel and a town of refuge, and no movement of the present age has troubled itself to redefine it. The dictionary records it as the proper name, distinct from the common noun for a well, that the reader may know the place where Israel sang over the water the LORD gave them in the desert.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the joyful provision of the LORD, who gathers His people and gives them water, and draws a song from their lips. With joy shall ye draw water out of the wells of salvation (Isa 12:3). He who said, Gather the people together, and I will give them water, and brought forth the spring at the staves of the princes, is the same who is the fountain of living waters; and the song over the well of the wilderness is a foretaste of the new song of the redeemed, who drink of the river of His pleasures and praise Him for ever.

etymology: Hebrew ba‘al shālīshāh, “lord of Shalisha” or “place of the three,” a town in the land of Shalisha whence came a man with firstfruits unto Elisha.
biblical_def: Baal-shalisha is a town in the land of Shalisha, the region through which Saul passed when he sought his father’s asses (1Sam 9:4), made memorable in the days of Elisha by a deed of the prophet’s power and the LORD’s provision. “And there came a man from Baal-shalisha, and brought the man of God bread of the firstfruits, twenty loaves of barley, and full ears of corn in the husk” (2Ki 4:42). When Elisha bade his servant set it before the hundred men of the sons of the prophets, the servant marvelled; but the prophet said, “Give the people, that they may eat: for thus saith the LORD, They shall eat, and shall leave thereof” (2Ki 4:43). “So he set it before them, and they did eat, and left thereof, according to the word of the LORD” (2Ki 4:44). Thus a man bringing the firstfruits of his ground unto the man of God became the occasion of a miracle of multiplied bread, a sign that went before the greater feeding which the Lord Jesus wrought with a few loaves. The name carries the dark sound of Baal, the false god whose worship was Israel’s plague; yet here a faithful man honoured the true God with his firstfruits, and the LORD honoured his gift with increase. Baal-shalisha witnesses that the LORD is no man’s debtor, and that the little brought to Him in faith He multiplies, so that many eat and are filled and there is yet to spare.
webster_summary: A town in the land of Shalisha whence a man brought firstfruits to Elisha, who fed a hundred men.
webster_full: BAAL-SHALISHA, a town in the land of Shalisha, signifying “lord of Shalisha.”

It witnesses that the LORD multiplies the little brought to Him in faith.

corruption_summary: A place of Scripture; though its name bears the idol Baal, it witnesses that the LORD multiplies the firstfruits brought to Him in faith.
corruption_paragraphs: Baal-shalisha is a town of the land of Shalisha, and no movement of the present age has troubled itself to redefine it. Yet its very name preaches a real corruption of old: the name of Baal, the false god whose worship the LORD abhorred, was fastened even upon the towns of Israel, so deep had the plague of idolatry run in the land.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the LORD’s gracious provision and His honouring of faith, even in a place that bore an idol’s name. A man of Baal-shalisha brought the firstfruits of his ground unto the man of God, and the LORD multiplied the bread so that an hundred ate and left thereof. He who fed the prophets by Elisha is the same who fed the multitudes by His own hand, and who is Himself the bread of life. Where men turn from the dead Baal to the living God and bring Him their firstfruits, He fills the hungry and there is yet to spare.
roots_summary: From the Hebrew for “lord of Shalisha,” Baal-shalisha names the town whence firstfruits came to Elisha.
